questions.argument: "Tomato says my blade matches the cuts in the missing carrot. But look at his bruised skin - why trust someone that rotten?"
questions.explanation: Bruised skin does not answer the evidence about the blade. The gadget attacks Tomato instead of his argument. That is a Personal Attack.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Tomato claims he saw me spill the soup. He can't even decide whether he's a fruit or a vegetable, so how could he identify the culprit?"
questions.explanation: Being a fruit or a vegetable does not tell us whether Tomato saw the spill. The gadget attacks him instead of the evidence. That is a Personal Attack.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Chef, every utensil in the drawer believes Tomato stole the salt. They can't all be wrong!"
questions.explanation: Many utensils believing Tomato stole the salt is not evidence that he did. Popular beliefs can be wrong. That is Bandwagon.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "The forks, spoons, and knives all agree that gadgets make better witnesses than produce. You should believe my testimony over Tomato's."
questions.explanation: The gadgets agreeing about witnesses does not make them more reliable. Popularity is used in place of evidence. That is Bandwagon.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Please don't find me guilty of shredding the recipe, Chef. My handle is cracked, and I've already had such a difficult week!"
questions.explanation: A cracked handle and a difficult week do not show who shredded the recipe. The gadget asks for sympathy instead of giving evidence. That is Appeal to Pity.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "If you rule that I ruined the soup, I'll be thrown into the junk drawer. You wouldn't make me spend the rest of my life alone in the dark, would you?"
questions.explanation: Being sent to the junk drawer sounds sad, but it does not show who ruined the soup. Sympathy replaces evidence. That is Appeal to Pity.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "The refrigerator's ice dispenser says Tomato stole the flour. It's an expert at making ice, so its judgment about theft must be correct."
questions.explanation: Knowing how to make ice does not make someone an expert on theft. The gadget relies on an unrelated expert. That is Irrelevant Authority.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "The famous cake-decorating mixer says these scratches came from Tomato. Winning decorating contests makes it an expert in scratch identification!"
questions.explanation: Winning cake contests does not prove skill at identifying scratches. The gadget uses the wrong kind of expertise. That is Irrelevant Authority.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Chef, either you find Tomato guilty of spilling the oil, or you're saying that spilling oil on the floor is acceptable."
questions.explanation: The Chef can reject this accusation and still say spills are wrong. The gadget hides other possible choices. That is a False Dilemma.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Either Tomato stole the recipe, or I did. And I certainly didn't!" (Other kitchen residents also had access.)
questions.explanation: Other residents had access too. The gadget pretends only two suspects are possible. That is a False Dilemma.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "One tomato rolled off the counter yesterday. That proves tomatoes can't control where they go, so this Tomato must have rolled into the cake."
questions.explanation: One tomato falling does not prove all tomatoes lack control, or that this one hit the cake. The claim goes beyond the evidence. That is Hasty Generalization.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Tomato got one detail wrong about breakfast. Everything he says about the missing butter must be false."
questions.explanation: One wrong breakfast detail does not make every statement false. A tiny sample is used to judge everything. That is Hasty Generalization.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: Tomato: "The peeler should be kept in a protective cover." Peeler: "Tomato wants every gadget locked away forever so nobody can cook!"
questions.explanation: Tomato asked for a protective cover, not for every gadget to be locked away. The peeler attacks a changed version of the idea. That is a Straw Man.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: Tomato: "The crumbs on Toaster don't prove he stole the bread." Toaster: "Tomato thinks we should ignore all physical evidence!"
questions.explanation: Tomato questions one clue, not all physical evidence. Toaster changes his claim into an easier one to attack. That is a Straw Man.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Tomato asks why there's frosting caught in my whisk wires. But Chef, shouldn't we be discussing how filthy the oven is?"
questions.explanation: The dirty oven does not explain frosting on the whisk. A different issue distracts from the original question. That is a Red Herring.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Before we discuss whether my cord knocked over the milk, let's talk about Tomato leaving seeds all over your cutting board."
questions.explanation: Seeds on the board do not explain whether the cord spilled milk. Changing topics avoids the question. That is a Red Herring.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Tomato accuses me of dripping grease onto the recipe. But he dripped juice onto the shopping list yesterday!"
questions.explanation: Tomato dripping juice does not answer whether the gadget dripped grease. Pointing to similar wrongdoing avoids the criticism. That is Whataboutism.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Why should I answer Tomato's accusation that I blocked the sink? Tomato clogged the drain with his sticker last week!"
questions.explanation: Tomato blocking a drain before does not explain who blocked it now. The gadget points back at its accuser. That is Whataboutism.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "My account of the missing cheese is accurate because I'm a reliable grater. You can tell I'm reliable because my account is accurate."
questions.explanation: The grater calls its story accurate because it is reliable, then calls itself reliable because of the same story. Nothing new supports it. That is Circular Reasoning.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Tomato stole the basil because he's the thief in this kitchen. How do I know he's the thief? Because he stole the basil."
questions.explanation: Calling Tomato a thief just repeats the claim that he stole basil. A claim cannot prove itself. That is Circular Reasoning.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Tomato can't prove he never entered the pantry last night. Therefore, he entered it and stole the sugar."
questions.explanation: Not proving he stayed away does not prove Tomato entered the pantry. A missing disproof is treated as proof. That is Appeal to Ignorance.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Nobody has proved that my blades caused the scratches on the counter. That proves I'm innocent."
questions.explanation: Lack of proof that the blades made scratches does not prove they did not. Missing evidence is not proof of the opposite. That is Appeal to Ignorance.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "The soup curdled immediately after Tomato rolled beside the stove. His arrival must have curdled it!"
questions.explanation: The soup curdling after Tomato arrived does not prove he caused it. Happening afterward is not enough to show a cause. That is False Cause.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "The kitchen lights went out just after Tomato accused me. His accusation must have caused the power failure!"
questions.explanation: The lights failing after an accusation does not show the words caused it. The order of events is treated as proof. That is False Cause.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "If you let Tomato keep that stolen basil leaf, next he'll take a whole bunch, then empty the pantry, and soon there won't be a single ingredient left!"
questions.explanation: Keeping one leaf does not prove Tomato will empty the pantry. The gadget predicts bigger and bigger problems without support. That is a Slippery Slope.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "If Tomato is allowed to question my testimony, every ingredient will start questioning every gadget. Soon the kitchen will be in chaos and dinner will never be served!"
questions.explanation: Questioning one witness does not prove dinner will never be served. The gadget jumps to an extreme outcome. That is a Slippery Slope.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Chef, you throw away empty tomato cans. This Tomato has no filling inside him either, so you should throw him away too!"
questions.explanation: An empty can and a living tomato differ in ways that matter. Throwing away one does not justify throwing away the other. That is a False Analogy.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "You unplug a blender when it makes too much noise. Tomato is making noise by objecting, so you should silence him for the rest of the trial."
questions.explanation: A noisy blender and a defendant objecting have different roles. Unplugging one does not justify silencing the other. That is a False Analogy.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Chef said we need a sharp witness. My blades are sharp, so my testimony must be the most intelligent."
questions.explanation: Sharp means clever for a witness, but it means able to cut for blades. The gadget switches meanings to make its claim. That is Equivocation.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Tomato admitted he was ripe for an argument. Ripe means ready, so he admitted he was ready to start the fight!"
questions.explanation: Ripe for an argument is a figure of speech, not an admission of starting a fight. The meaning changes in the argument. That is Equivocation.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Tomato, where did you hide the measuring spoon you stole?" (It hasn't been established that Tomato stole it.)
questions.explanation: The question assumes Tomato stole the spoon before that has been proved. Answering where would accept that hidden claim. That is a Loaded Question.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Have you stopped sneaking into the refrigerator after midnight?" (Either yes or no accepts that Tomato previously did this.)
questions.explanation: Yes or no would accept that Tomato used to sneak into the fridge. That has not been proved. That is a Loaded Question.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "This camera image shows Tomato beside the broken plate!" (The gadget skips the next frame, which shows its own cord pulling the plate off the counter.)
questions.explanation: The gadget shows one frame and hides the next frame with important evidence about its cord. Choosing only helpful evidence is Cherry-Picking.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "The salt shaker heard Tomato threaten to 'crush' Garlic!" (Ignores the rest of the conversation: Tomato was reading the chef's recipe aloud.)
questions.explanation: The full conversation shows Tomato reading a recipe. Leaving that out changes what the words seem to mean. That is Cherry-Picking.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "Show us a photo proving you were in the fruit bowl when the spill happened." Tomato provides one. "A photo isn't enough. Now you need a video!"
questions.explanation: Tomato supplies the requested photo, then the gadget demands a video. It changes the rule after the original demand is met. That is Moving the Goalposts.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.argument: "I'll accept your innocence if one witness confirms you never touched the oven." The kettle confirms it. "Actually, I'll need three witnesses - and none of them can be appliances."
questions.explanation: The gadget asks for one witness, gets one, then demands three and excludes appliances. It changes the standard after it is met. That is Moving the Goalposts.
questions.source: Project plan Section 6.1; explanation adapted for gameplay

questions.explanation: The speaker attacks a person's traits instead of checking the evidence. Those traits do not prove the claim wrong. That is a Personal Attack.
